title: My God, My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?
summary: A sufferer cries out to a God who seems absent, remembering that Israel's fathers trusted and were delivered while he is mocked, surrounded by enemies pictured as bulls, lions, and dogs, and brought to the dust of death. At the lowest point the prayer breaks into the declaration that God has answered. The psalm ends in widening praise: in the assembly, among all Israel, to the ends of the earth, and to generations not yet born.
story: Psalm 22 follows two royal psalms in which the king is crowned and victorious, and it plunges into the opposite experience: a man abandoned, exposed, and near death. It is then followed by Psalm 23, the quiet song of the shepherd. The sequence (the crowned king, the forsaken sufferer, the shepherded guest at God's table) has struck many readers as deliberate. Psalm 22 is the Old Testament passage most quoted and echoed in the Gospel accounts of Jesus' crucifixion, and Jesus himself prayed its first line from the cross. It is one of the places where the whole Bible's story most clearly bends toward the cross and the resurrection.
historical:
The heading reads For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Doe of the Dawn.” A Psalm of David. The tune name probably refers to a melody known to the temple musicians; its meaning is uncertain. Traditional readers attribute the psalm to David, and no episode in his recorded life matches it closely, which has led some to read it as David speaking beyond his own experience. Many modern scholars see it as an individual lament of unknown date and author, perhaps shaped for repeated use in worship, and some think the closing section (verses 27 to 31), with its vision of the nations and the dead worshiping, reflects a later, post-exilic horizon. Others defend its unity, noting how the praise answers the complaint point by point.

The psalm names no historical event, and that very generality made it usable by any sufferer in Israel. Its images of animals and of a body failing are poetic, drawn from a world of wild bulls, lions, and scavenging dogs, and they describe the experience of being surrounded and overwhelmed as much as any specific scene.
cultural:
Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for rich pasture and strong cattle (Amos 4:1), so the bulls of Bashan are powerful, well-fed, and menacing. Dogs in ancient Israel were not pets but half-wild scavengers that roamed town edges and fed on the dead (1 Kings 21:23-24), which makes their encircling of the sufferer especially horrifying. A potsherd was a fragment of broken pottery, the driest and most worthless thing in a household. Dividing a condemned or dying person's clothing was a practical custom: garments were valuable, and those who had power over the victim claimed them.

The second half reflects Israel's worship. A person rescued from trouble would fulfill vows (promises made in distress) by offering a thanksgiving sacrifice at the sanctuary, and the meat of such a sacrifice was shared in a meal (Leviticus 7:11-16). So when verse 26 says the poor will eat and be satisfied, it pictures the rescued sufferer hosting a feast of thanksgiving that includes the needy.
literary: The psalm is an individual lament that turns into thanksgiving, and it is built with great care. The first half (verses 1 to 21) alternates between complaint and trust: God is far (verses 1 and 2), yet he is holy and trustworthy (3 to 5); I am a worm (6 to 8), yet you brought me from the womb (9 and 10). Three times the sufferer begs God not to be far (verses 1, 11, 19). The enemies close in as bulls, lions, and dogs, and the rescue plea names them in reverse: sword and dogs, lion, wild oxen (verses 20 and 21). Then, in the middle of verse 21, the Hebrew shifts abruptly, “You have answered me”, and the psalm turns. The praise that follows moves outward in widening circles: my brothers, the great assembly, all Israel, the ends of the earth, the dead, and a people yet unborn.

outline.t: Why have you forsaken me? The God who delivered our fathers
Mocked by all, yet held since birth
Surrounded by bulls, lions, and dogs; poured out like water
Be not far off: you have answered me
The nations, the dead, and the unborn will worship

doctrines.note: The psalm gives the faithful words for the experience of God's absence, and it doesn't rush past the complaint. It shows that crying why to God is itself an act of faith, addressed to my God.

Christians have seen in this psalm the shape of Christ's suffering on the cross: forsaken, mocked, stripped, and exposed, yet answered by God. The New Testament uses it to interpret his death, and the psalm's turn to praise anticipates the resurrection.

The final verses envision all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD and all the families of the nations bowing before him, echoing God's promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3).
Verse 28 declares that dominion belongs to the LORD and he rules over the nations. Even in the depths of forsakenness, the psalm ends by confessing that God reigns.

words.note: Azav, to leave or forsake, to abandon. It is used of leaving a place, a person, or a covenant. The question of verse 1 is not whether God exists but why the God who is my God has left me. The cry is relational, not philosophical, which is why it can be prayed.

Aryeh, lion. It appears in verses 13 and 21, and the standard Hebrew text also has it in verse 16, where it reads like a lion, my hands and my feet. The ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint, made by Jewish scholars before Christ) reads they dug or pierced, and a Hebrew Psalms fragment from Nahal Hever near the Dead Sea has a form that may support a verb. Translations differ; see the hard question below.

Qahal, assembly or congregation, the gathered people of God. In verse 22 and verse 25 the rescued sufferer praises God in the assembly. The Greek translation often renders this word ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for the church.

Ani, afflicted, poor, humble. It describes someone bowed down by trouble or oppression. Verse 24 grounds the whole turn to praise in this: God has not despised the torment of the afflicted. The Psalms repeatedly show God's attention bending toward the lowly.

christ: No psalm is woven more deeply into the story of Jesus' death. From the cross he cried its first line in his own Aramaic: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34). The Gospels describe passersby shaking their heads (Matthew 27:39) and the leaders mocking, He trusts in God, let God deliver him (Matthew 27:43, echoing verse 8). John says the soldiers divided his garments and cast lots for his tunic to fulfill the Scripture, and he quotes verse 18: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing” (John 19:24). Hebrews 2:12 puts verse 22 on the lips of the risen Christ, who is not ashamed to call his people brothers. Jewish readers have generally understood the psalm as the prayer of David or of any righteous sufferer, and Christians agree that it was that first. The New Testament's claim is that Jesus prayed it as its fullest speaker: the righteous sufferer who was truly forsaken, truly answered in resurrection, and whose rescue brings the ends of the earth to worship.

hard.q: Does verse 16 really say they pierced my hands and feet, or is that a Christian reading imposed on the text?
hard.a: The difficulty is textual. The standard Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text) reads a phrase that means like a lion, my hands and my feet, which lacks a verb and is hard to make sense of; Jewish translations often supply a verb, reading it as lions mauling or pinning the hands and feet. The Septuagint, the Greek translation made by Jewish scholars before the Christian era, reads they dug my hands and feet, and several other ancient versions read a verb as well. A Hebrew fragment of the Psalms from Nahal Hever, from around the first century AD, has a spelling that many scholars take as a verb, though its meaning is also debated. Christian translations like the BSB follow the versions and read pierced, arguing that the Hebrew letters differ only slightly and that the Greek evidence predates any Christian dispute. Others argue that the Masoretic reading, though difficult, should be kept and that the lion image fits the surrounding verses. It is worth noting that none of the Gospels quotes verse 16, so the psalm's connection to the crucifixion does not rest on this verse.

questions: The psalmist calls God my God even while asking why God has forsaken him. What does that suggest about honest prayer in times when God feels absent?
Jesus prayed this psalm from the cross. How does that change the way you understand either the psalm or his death?
The psalm moves from one person's rescue to the ends of the earth and a people yet unborn. How might your own story of God's help reach people you will never meet?
